summary: Specifies DHCP options that deliver timezone information either as a POSIX timezone string or a timezone database name. The old DHCPv4 time offset option is deprecated.

eli5.summary: When a device joins a network, the network can tell it what time zone it is in. This note adds two ways to say it and retires the old simple way.

questions: how to set time zone with dhcp
what is the dhcp timezone option
is the dhcp time offset option deprecated
subtitle: Two DHCP options that tell a host its timezone, as a POSIX string or a timezone database name, replacing the bare time offset.

tldr.problem: The old DHCPv4 time offset option only gives a number of seconds from UTC. A client cannot tell from it whether daylight saving time applies, when it starts or ends, or what the zone is called.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4833 defines two options for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6: one carries a POSIX TZ string, the other carries the name of an entry in the TZ database. Clients that know the TZ name prefer it.
tldr.outcome: The DHCPv4 time offset option is deprecated in favour of the new options. Servers that implement one new option SHOULD implement both.

today: RFC 4833 is a Proposed Standard from April 2007. It updates RFC 2132, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Time Offset Is Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 2132 already lets a DHCP server give a client its timezone, but only as an offset in seconds from UTC. That is not enough for the client to know whether it is currently in daylight saving time (DST), or when to switch into and out of it. It also cannot yield a human-readable abbreviation such as EST or EDT.

The RFC points out an awkward workaround: the server would have to time lease expirations to the start or end of DST, which it calls a self stress test. RFC 4833 instead lets the server hand over richer timezone information once, using two common methods: POSIX TZ strings and names from the TZ database.

The RFC also considers and sets aside the iCalendar VTIMEZONE element. There is no global registry of its identifiers, a full entry would take 300 octets upwards, and the authors knew of no operating system that natively uses it.
sections.eli5: Knowing only how far your clock is from the world clock is like knowing your seat number but not the show time. The new options also say when the clocks change.

sections.title: The New Options in DHCPv4 and DHCPv6
sections.content:
For DHCPv4, two options are defined: option 100 (PCode) carries an IEEE 1003.1 POSIX string, and option 101 (TCode) carries a reference to the TZ database. Each has a one-octet Len followed by the string. The strings are NOT terminated by an ASCII NULL. IANA allocated both codes under the process of RFC 2939.

The DHCPv6 versions have the same semantics and content, adjusted for how DHCPv6 encodes options. OPTION_NEW_POSIX_TIMEZONE is option code 41 and OPTION_NEW_TZDB_TIMEZONE is option code 42. Each is an option code, an option-length and then the string.
sections.eli5: Each option is a small labelled envelope with a length and a short piece of text inside. IPv4 and IPv6 networks use different label numbers for the same two envelopes.

sections.title: The POSIX String and the TZ Name
sections.content:
The TZ POSIX string is a string suitable for the TZ variable in POSIX section 8.3, except that it may not begin with a colon. The RFC's example is EST5EDT4,M3.2.0/02:00,M11.1.0/02:00: five hours behind UTC normally, four during DST, with DST running from the second Sunday in March at 02:00 local time to the first Sunday in November at 02:00. The abbreviation is EST, or EDT during DST. Clients and servers implementing other timezone options MUST support this option for basic compatibility.

The TZ Name is the name field of a zone line in the TZ database, for example Europe/Zurich. It is only useful if the client already has a copy of the database; configuring that copy is out of scope. A client that supports the option SHOULD prefer it to the POSIX string if it recognizes the name, and MUST ignore the option if it does not.
sections.eli5: One option is a recipe for the clock rules. The other is just the name of a place, like Europe/Zurich, which only helps if your computer already has the list of places.

sections.title: How Servers and Clients Use Them
sections.content:
The RFC presumes the server has some way to know which timezone a client is in; an obvious approach is to associate a subnet or group of subnets with a timezone. The TZ Name is better for most uses and gives accuracy over longer historical periods. The POSIX string needs no regularly updated database, so it may suit small-footprint applications that are expertly maintained.

So that clients need not request both options, servers that implement either option SHOULD implement the other. A basic server can pass the values on without parsing them; a more advanced one might validate names against its own copy of the database or derive POSIX strings from names.

The effect on running applications is not specified, but the RFC warns that many applications read the timezone only at start-up or inherit it from a parent process, so existing processes may ignore a change. Servers may need to update the string when local jurisdictions change their rules, and a lease time might be kept short if a change is anticipated. If a lease expires and no new information arrives, the client MAY keep using the timezone it was given.
sections.eli5: The network picks the right answer for each part of the building. Running programs may not notice a change in time zone until they restart, just like a wall clock you forgot to look at.

sections.title: Deprecating the Time Offset Option
sections.content:
Because the new options do everything the old IPv4 time offset option (tag 2) did and more, and to keep IPv4 and IPv6 consistent, the old option is deprecated. This is why RFC 4833 is marked as updating RFC 2132.

Current implementations that support the time offset option SHOULD implement the new ones too. Other implementations SHOULD implement the new options and SHOULD NOT implement the time offset option. During the transition a client that already uses the time offset option MAY request both.
sections.eli5: The old simple option is being retired. Newer devices should ask for the better ones, and older devices can ask for both while everyone catches up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could give a client wrong timezone information. People might miss meetings, machinery might act at the wrong time, and wall-clock tools such as cron could run jobs early, late, repeatedly or not at all around a DST transition. The RFC suggests that the client operating system might do well to confirm timezone changes with a human.

Clients using the POSIX option should beware of unusual characters such as control characters in the abbreviations, which might trigger security-relevant bugs in applications. They should also be suspicious of any setting whose UTC offset exceeds 25 hours, the POSIX limit with the default daylight-saving offset. The RFC notes that the maximum offset in practice was 14 hours at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: If someone fed your computer the wrong time zone, you could show up at the wrong hour. So the computer should be careful about odd answers.
